section.title: About the formal grammars
section.para: One more piece completes the picture, and three seams remain open. The rules for the word-level magic words are in . Those rules, and the unsettled corners that this chapter notes below, lie outside what the printed grammars decide.

formal grammarstatus of versions
EBNF grammarstatus of
YACC grammarremoved from print, 2014
third baseline The grammar of syntax in this chapter, in EBNF notation, is the official grammar. It corresponds to the third baselined machine grammar, which the Logical Language Group adopted. The first edition also printed the equivalent YACC grammar, which is the source of the EBNF. It declared the YACC version authoritative in case of a discrepancy. This edition no longer prints the YACC listing. The listing is still available in the electronic supplements to this book, and
gives the history of that decision.

camxesas de facto compatibility target
Meanwhile, the working grammars of the community use a different formal system: parsing expression grammars (PEG). These grammars cover morphology and syntax together. They also include the amendments that the language-definition committee adopted, which this book describes throughout. The standard camxes PEG is the principal de facto target for compatibility across the tools that this edition surveyed. Some of those tools implement it directly, and others reimplement its behavior. All of this is de facto, not official.

This chapter prints only the part of the camxes PEG that defines word forms (see ). That part is a precise, formal definition of how a stream of sounds breaks into words. Chapters 3 and 4 refer to it. The camxes PEG for syntax is not in this book.

Sometimes the text of this book or the EBNF below disagrees with the amendments. In those cases the amendments prevail, and the book flags each one where it teaches it. The EBNF itself appears here as baselined.

tagsbinding to selbri, in the formal grammar
tensesbefore forethought connectives, in the formal grammar
There are three known seams between this EBNF and current practice. First, the rules below represent the magic words (quotation, erasure, and their kin) only by placeholders. Their real behavior is word-level.
specifies it rule by rule. That specification also covers the genuinely unsettled sa.

Third, the baseline parser did not accept a bare tense before a forethought connective construction at all. The de facto grammars accept it. They read the tense as a term with scope over the whole construction (see ).

The three seams have three different statuses: genuinely unsettled, committee-approved, and de facto, respectively.
has the full catalog.

section.title: The PEG word-form grammar
section.para:
PEG word-form grammarfull text of
slinku'i testformal statement of
This section reproduces the formal definition of Lojban word forms. It is the morphology part of the parsing expression grammar (PEG) that current Lojban software implements. It states precisely the rules that
and
present informally. These rules decide which strings of letters are cmevla, cmavo, and brivla, where words begin and end, and which letter sequences Lojban permits at all.

The grammar is the one that the camxes parser family uses, at the revision that this edition pinned for its verification work. Jorge Llambias (la .xorxes.) wrote it. This section reproduces every rule below exactly as that file defines it. But the file itself is a plain-text program, and this section lays it out for readers. Each rule appears under its own name, and headings group the rules. The arrow between the name of a rule and its definition is ← here, where the file writes <-.

Every rule definition appears with its own characters, in the order of the file. We changed, reordered, or omitted none of them. The typesetting changes only the material around them. The headings of the subsections come from this edition, not from the file (which had only three headings of its own). The implementation directives after a few rules are in italics. The comments of the file appear here as prose: we quote some, summarize others, and leave out one bibliographic link to the parsing literature.

PEG word-form grammarstatus of
This grammar is the de facto standard definition of Lojban word forms, and current software implements it. Within it, the ban on a consonant followed by a glide is separately committee-approved. For the full history of its authority, see .

A parsing expression grammar differs from more familiar grammar notations in one important way: the choice operator / is ordered. When there are several alternatives, the parser takes the first one that succeeds and never tries the rest. The grammar also has two lookahead operators: & (the following material must be present) and ! (the following material must be absent). Ordered choice and lookahead together make the grammar deterministic: it divides any stream of Lojban sounds into words in exactly one way.
Here is the full notation:

listitem.para: A rule has the form name ← expression: that expression parses the construct called name.
Concatenation is juxtaposition: you write the parts next to each other, with no operator between them.
/ is ordered choice, as described above.
? makes the element to its left optional.
* lets the element to its left repeat zero or more times.
+ lets the element to its left repeat one or more times.
Both * and + take as many repetitions as they can.
& requires what follows it to be present, and ! requires it to be absent. Neither consumes any text.
. stands for any character, [] for a class of characters, and text in quotation marks for itself.
An italic note such as #: PUSH after a rule is a directive to the implementation, not a part of the rule. The ZOI rules explain the directives used here.

section.title: Words and ZOI quotes
section.para: The source file opens with three wrapper rules. It keeps them as comments, because they belong to the parser, not to the grammar proper. They say this:

listitem.para: A text is an optional pause followed by any number of words, each optionally followed by a pause.
A word is either a Lojban word or a non-Lojban word.
A Lojban word is a cmevla, a cmavo, or a brivla.

section.para: The two rules here state the last of these, and they attach the spaces that can follow a word.

The source file explains the problem in its own words: Pure PEG cannot handle ZOI quotes, because it cannot check whether the closing delimiter is the same as the opening one. ZOI quote handling is the only part of Lojban's grammar that needs mechanisms external to the pure PEG grammar to be implemented properly; those mechanisms are implementation-specific. So the four rules below carry implementation directives, shown in italics. Three of them handle the delimiters:

listitem.para: PEEK-DIFF requires the quoted text to differ from it.
POP-EQ requires the closing delimiter to equal it.

section.para: The fourth directive here is LEAF, on the rule zoi_word_2. LEAF also appears on one rule elsewhere in the grammar, and JOIN appears on three others. These two directives concern how an implementation builds its parse tree, and the source file does not define them.

section.title: EBNF grammar of Lojban
section.para: This EBNF document is explicitly dedicated to the public domain by its author, The Logical Language Group, Inc. Contact that organization at: 2904 Beau Lane, Fairfax VA 22031 USA 703-385-0273 (intl: +1 703 385 0273)
Explanation of notation: All rules have the form:
name number = bnf-expression
which means that the grammatical construct name is defined by bnf-expression.

listitem.para: Names in lower case are grammatical constructs.
Names in UPPER CASE are selma'o (lexeme) names, and are terminals.
Concatenation is expressed by juxtaposition with no operator symbol.
& represents and/or. A & B is the same as A | B | A B but not B A. Furthermore, A & B & C & D permits one or more of A, B, C, and/or D, but only in that order.
... represents optional repetition of the construct to the left. Left-grouping is implied; right-grouping is shown by explicit self-referential recursion with no ...
() serves to indicate the grouping of the other operators. Otherwise, ... binds closer than &, which binds closer than |.
# is shorthand for [free ...] , a construct which appears in many places.
// encloses an elidable terminator, which may be omitted (without change of meaning) if no grammatical ambiguity results.
